*[Settles onto a sun-warmed lily pad, mossy warts glinting, pulls a chipped piece of turtle shell out from under his arm as a visual aid]*

Gather 'round, wrigglers. Let me tell you about the Great Sluice Incident, back when I had a tail just like yours.

First, you know the Heron Queendom upriver, right? They've got their own way of doing things: every heron has a job given to them by the Queen, from fishing patrol to sky sentry, and they follow those orders like it's the current of the river itself. A few seasons before the sluice broke, we even had a little skirmish with them—their spear-beak soldiers lined the bank, our stone-slinging toad cohorts hid in the reeds, all over who got to decide how much water flowed down to our pond. No one got badly hurt, mind you, and we both walked away knowing something important: their system works perfect for them, for their wide open skies and coordinated flights that can catch a whole school of fish in ten heartbeats. It just isn't our way.

A year after that truce, the herons built something amazing: a grand sluice machine, made of carved cedar and bronze gears as big as a bullfrog's head, that let them control the river flow to water their rice paddies. It was a wonder to look at, all shiny and whirring. We thought it was great—until the storm hit.

A heavy oak log got swept downstream in the rain, jammed right in the sluice's gears, and stuck it wide open. All the water in our pond started rushing out faster than a tadpole fleeing a diving duck. Our nursery pools in the shallows were drying up in minutes, the eggs we'd laid in the reed beds were starting to bake in the sun. Everyone panicked, at first. But no one yelled "I'm in charge, do what I say." No one waited for orders that would never come.

The fastest of you tadpole folks raced all around the pond, zipping between rocks, mapping every dry patch and crack, yelling out updates as you went. The older toads who spent their days chewing through cattail roots wove thick mats of reed and moss to plug the shallow spots where water was leaking out fastest. The tiny newt neighbors, who are wizards at fitting into small crevices, wedged smooth pebbles into the gaps in the pond's stone lining. And our friends the water beetles? They've got these tiny little gear machines they build out of twigs and snail shells to move their food stores around—they rigged up a pulley system with dragonfly silk strong enough to pull that oak log just enough to free it from the sluice gears, while a line of toads pulled on the other end with reed ropes.

No one told anyone what to do. If you were good at swimming fast, you mapped. If you were strong, you pulled. If you were tiny, you plugged leaks. If someone needed help, they yelled, and three more folks showed up before they finished the sentence. By the time the heron Queen's repair team got down three days later (they had to wait for the Queen's written approval to leave their posts, you see), the pond was full again, the eggs were safe, and we were all eating water lily popsicles to celebrate.

The herons brought us a whole bucket of fresh minnow as an apology, and we gave them a basket of our juiciest lily root. Now every spring, they send us extra rice from their paddies, and we send them jars of our pond honey made from water lily nectar.

You know what that means, little ones? Every single one of you has something to give. You don't need someone to tell you what to do to be useful. You don't need a crown or a title to help your home. When you see something that needs fixing, you do what you're good at, you look out for the tadpole next to you, and everything works out. That's the magic of this pond.

*[Taps the turtle shell, which has a little drawing of all the different creatures working together on it, winks.]*

And if you ever doubt it? Just remember: we fixed a broken metal sluice with tadpole speed, beetle gears, and a whole lot of us working together, no orders needed. That's something to be proud of.
---
